title: Lists
overview: Variables store one value. But what if you need to store 100 student marks? Or 50 product names? Lists are Python's most versatile data structure — an ordered collection that can hold multiple items of any type.

blocks.content: A **list** is a collection of items stored in a single variable. Instead of creating 10 variables for 10 marks, you create one list.
Lists are defined with square brackets `[]`, with items separated by commas.

blocks.title: Try It — Creating Lists
blocks.code:
# A list of student marks
marks = [78, 92, 85, 67, 95]

# A list of names
students = ["Priya", "Ravi", "Meera", "Arjun"]

# A mixed list
profile = ["Lakshanya", 20, "Chennai", True]

print(marks)
print(students)
print(len(marks))   # Number of items

blocks.content: To access a specific item, use its **index** inside square brackets. Python counting starts at **0**, not 1.

blocks.title: Try It — Indexing
blocks.code:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry", "date"]

print(fruits[0])   # First item
print(fruits[1])   # Second item
print(fruits[-1])  # Last item (negative index!)
print(fruits[-2])  # Second from last

blocks.content: **Negative indexing** is one of Python's clever features. `-1` always gives the last item, `-2` the second-to-last, and so on. You don't need to know the length to access the end.

analogy.title: Train Coaches
analogy.description: A train has coaches numbered starting from 0. Coach 0 is the engine, coach 1 is next, and so on. Passenger -1 is always in the last coach. Python lists work exactly like this — ordered, numbered from 0, with negative indices for the end.
bullets: Coaches are numbered from the engine: 1, 2, 3, 4...
Your ticket tells you exactly which coach and seat to find.
The position (index) is how you locate your exact spot on the train.
analogy.highlightCard: List indexing lets you access any element by its position — starting at 0.

visualization.title: List Indexing
bullets: List index starts at 0, not 1 — the first item is at position [0].
Use list[index] to access any specific element directly.
Negative indices count from the end: list[-1] is always the last item.
visualization.highlightCard: trains[0] is the first coach, trains[-1] is the last — indexing is instant access.

highlights: coaches[0] accesses 'Engine' — the first item at index 0.
coaches[2] accesses the third item — index 2 is always position 3.
coaches[-1] accesses the last item, regardless of how long the list is.
code.highlightCard: Indexing gives you direct, instant access to any element in a list.

reflection.question: If a list has 6 items, what is the index of the last item?
reflection.answer: 5 — or -1 using negative indexing. Python starts at 0, so items are at indices 0 through 5.

blocks.stage1Transition: Python lists are like trains — each item has a numbered position. Let's see how indexing works.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how list indexing looks in Python.
blocks.takeaway: Train coaches and list indices work the same way — each position has a number, and you use that number to access exactly what you need. Python lists count from 0.

blocks.title: Student Roster
blocks.instructions: You have a class roster: students = ["Aisha", "Rohan", "Divya", "Karthik", "Sneha"]. Print: the first student, the last student, and the total number of students.
blocks.starterCode:
students = ["Aisha", "Rohan", "Divya", "Karthik", "Sneha"]

# Print first student
print("First:", )
# Print last student
print("Last:", )
# Print total count
print("Total:", )
blocks.solution:
students = ["Aisha", "Rohan", "Divya", "Karthik", "Sneha"]

print("First:", students[0])
print("Last:", students[-1])
print("Total:", len(students))
blocks.hint: Use [0] for first, [-1] for last, and len() for the count.

blocks.content: Lists in Python are **mutable** — you can change them after creation. Add items, remove items, change items. This is what makes lists so useful.

**Changing an item:** Use the index with `=`.

**Slicing:** Get a portion of the list with `[start:stop]`.

blocks.title: Try It — Modifying and Slicing
blocks.code:
marks = [70, 85, 90, 60, 75]

# Change the 4th mark
marks[3] = 80
print("Updated:", marks)

# Slicing: first 3 marks
print("First 3:", marks[0:3])

# Slicing: last 2 marks
print("Last 2:", marks[-2:])

blocks.content: Slicing `[start:stop]` returns items from index `start` up to but **not including** `stop`. Leaving either empty means 'go to the beginning/end'.

blocks.title: Try It — List Concatenation and Repetition
blocks.code:
list1 = [1, 2, 3]
list2 = [4, 5, 6]

# Combine lists
combined = list1 + list2
print(combined)

# Repeat a list
repeated = [0] * 5
print(repeated)

analogy.title: Playlist
analogy.description: A music playlist lets you add songs, remove songs, rearrange the order, and play just a portion. Python lists are exactly like playlists — ordered, changeable, and you can get any slice of them.
bullets: You pick a range of songs to listen to — not the full playlist.
Tracks 2 through 4 play: you get 3 songs from one selection.
The rest of the playlist is unaffected — you're just viewing a slice.
analogy.highlightCard: Slicing extracts a portion of a list without modifying the original.

visualization.title: List Slice [1:4]
bullets: list[start:stop] extracts items from start up to (but not including) stop.
Omit start to begin from the first element: list[:3].
Omit stop to go until the last element: list[2:].
visualization.highlightCard: playlist[1:4] gives you items at index 1, 2, 3 — stop index is excluded.

highlights: playlist[1:4] extracts items at positions 1, 2, and 3 — not 4.
The original list is unchanged — slicing creates a new list.
Add a third value for step: playlist[::2] picks every other song.
code.highlightCard: Slicing is powerful — extract any portion of any list in a single clean expression.

reflection.question: What does marks[2:5] return from a list of 7 items?
reflection.answer: Items at indices 2, 3, and 4 — three items starting from index 2, stopping before index 5.

blocks.stage1Transition: Python's slice notation lets you extract any sub-section of a list. Let's see how.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how list slicing works in Python.
blocks.takeaway: Like choosing a range of songs from a playlist, list slicing extracts any sub-section you choose. The start is included, the stop is excluded, and the original is never modified.

blocks.title: Top 3 Scores
blocks.instructions: Given scores = [45, 78, 92, 55, 88, 96, 70], you want to extract the first 3 scores, update the second score from 78 to 85, and print the updated list and the first-3 slice.
blocks.starterCode:
scores = [45, 78, 92, 55, 88, 96, 70]

# Update second score to 85


# Print full updated list
print("Updated:", scores)

# Print first 3 scores
print("First 3:", )
blocks.solution:
scores = [45, 78, 92, 55, 88, 96, 70]

scores[1] = 85

print("Updated:", scores)
print("First 3:", scores[0:3])
blocks.hint: scores[1] = 85 updates index 1. scores[0:3] gives the first 3 items.

blocks.content: Python lists come with built-in methods — actions you can call on a list directly using `list.method()` syntax.

blocks.title: Try It — Essential List Methods
blocks.code:
cart = ["laptop", "mouse", "keyboard"]

# Add to end
cart.append("monitor")
print("After append:", cart)

# Insert at position
cart.insert(1, "USB hub")
print("After insert:", cart)

# Remove by value
cart.remove("mouse")
print("After remove:", cart)

# Remove and return last item
last = cart.pop()
print("Popped:", last)
print("After pop:", cart)
blocks.expectedOutput:
After append: ['laptop', 'mouse', 'keyboard', 'monitor']
After insert: ['laptop', 'USB hub', 'mouse', 'keyboard', 'monitor']
After remove: ['laptop', 'USB hub', 'keyboard', 'monitor']
Popped: monitor
After pop: ['laptop', 'USB hub', 'keyboard']

blocks.title: Try It — Sorting and Searching
blocks.code:
numbers = [5, 2, 8, 1, 9, 3]

# Sort in ascending order
numbers.sort()
print("Sorted:", numbers)

# Reverse
numbers.reverse()
print("Reversed:", numbers)

# Search
print("Index of 8:", numbers.index(8))
print("Count of 1:", numbers.count(1))
blocks.expectedOutput:
Sorted: [1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 9]
Reversed: [9, 8, 5, 3, 2, 1]
Index of 8: 1
Count of 1: 1

analogy.title: Library Book Shelf
analogy.description: A library shelf has specific operations: add a new book (append), insert between two books (insert), return a book (remove/pop), sort alphabetically (sort), and find where a book is (index). List methods mirror these exact real-world operations.
bullets: Adding a new book: place it at the end of the shelf.
Removing a book: take it off the shelf and the others close the gap.
Searching for a book: scan the shelf to find its exact position.
analogy.highlightCard: List methods let you add, remove, sort, and search — all built in.

visualization.title: List Methods by Purpose
bullets: append() adds a new item to the end of the list.
remove() deletes the first occurrence of a specific value.
sort() rearranges items in ascending order, in place.
visualization.highlightCard: append, remove, sort, len — four methods every Python list user must know.

highlights: books.append('Python Crash Course') adds the book to the end.
books.remove('Old Book') deletes the first matching item.
books.sort() rearranges items alphabetically — it modifies the list in place.
code.highlightCard: List methods are built-in tools — you never need to write these operations from scratch.

reflection.question: What is the difference between remove() and pop()?
reflection.answer: remove() deletes by value. pop() deletes by index (default: last item) and returns the removed item.
options: remove() deletes by value; pop() deletes by index and returns the item

blocks.stage1Transition: Python lists have built-in methods for every operation you need. Let's explore them.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how the most common list methods look in Python.
blocks.takeaway: A library shelf demonstrates every list operation: add a book (append), remove one (remove), reorganize (sort), and count the collection (len). Python lists have all of these built in.

blocks.title: Manage a Waitlist
blocks.instructions: You manage a college event waitlist = ["Arun", "Bina", "Carlos", "Divya"]. Do these operations in order: 1) Add 'Esha' at the end. 2) Remove 'Carlos' from the list. 3) Sort alphabetically. 4) Print the final list and its length.
blocks.starterCode:
waitlist = ["Arun", "Bina", "Carlos", "Divya"]

# 1. Add Esha

# 2. Remove Carlos

# 3. Sort

# 4. Print result
print("Waitlist:", waitlist)
print("Count:", len(waitlist))
blocks.solution:
waitlist = ["Arun", "Bina", "Carlos", "Divya"]

waitlist.append("Esha")
waitlist.remove("Carlos")
waitlist.sort()

print("Waitlist:", waitlist)
print("Count:", len(waitlist))
blocks.hint: Use .append(), .remove(), and .sort() in sequence. sort() sorts in place.

keyTakeaways.text: Lists store multiple items in one variable, defined with square brackets: [].
Indexing starts at 0. The last item is at index -1.
Slicing [start:stop] extracts a portion — stop is excluded.
Lists are mutable — you can change items using index assignment.
append() adds to the end; insert(i, x) adds at position i.
remove() deletes by value; pop() removes by index and returns the item.
sort() sorts in place; sorted() returns a new sorted list without modifying the original.

whatYouLearned: How to create lists and access items by index
How to modify lists: change, add, remove
Essential list methods: append, insert, remove, pop, sort, reverse, index, count

quiz.question: What is the index of the first item in a Python list?
quiz.explanation: Python uses zero-based indexing. The first item is at index 0, the second at index 1, and so on.

quiz.question: What does items[-2] return?
quiz.explanation: Negative indices count from the end. -1 is the last item, -2 is the second-to-last, and so on.

quiz.question: What is the difference between append() and insert()?
options: append() adds to the end; insert(i, x) adds at index i
quiz.answer: append() adds to the end; insert(i, x) adds at index i
quiz.explanation: append() always adds to the end. insert() lets you specify exactly where to put the new item.

quiz.question: What does nums[1:4] return from [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]?
quiz.explanation: Slicing [1:4] starts at index 1 (value 20) and goes up to but not including index 4 (value 50). So it returns indices 1, 2, 3: [20, 30, 40].

quiz.question: What does pop() do when called without arguments?
options: Removes and returns the last item
quiz.answer: Removes and returns the last item
quiz.explanation: pop() without arguments removes the last item and returns it, so you can use the removed value. pop(0) would remove the first item.

problems.title: List Statistics
problems.description:
Given temperatures = [28, 32, 25, 30, 35, 22, 29], calculate and print:
- Minimum temperature (use min())
- Maximum temperature (use max())
- Average temperature
- Total count
problems.solution:
temperatures = [28, 32, 25, 30, 35, 22, 29]

print(f"Min: {min(temperatures)}")
print(f"Max: {max(temperatures)}")
print(f"Average: {sum(temperatures) / len(temperatures)}")
print(f"Count: {len(temperatures)}")

problems.title: Reverse a List Without reverse()
problems.description:
Given data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], reverse it without using the .reverse() method or [::-1]. Use a loop to build a new reversed list.

Expected output:
[5, 4, 3, 2, 1]
problems.starterCode:
data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
reversed_list = []

# Use a loop to reverse
problems.solution:
data = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
reversed_list = []

for i in range(len(data) - 1, -1, -1):
    reversed_list.append(data[i])

print(reversed_list)
